text: You are driving in a built-up area and there are no speed limit signs. What is the maximum speed you may travel?
options: 40 km/h
50 km/h
60 km/h
70 km/h
explanation: The default limit in a built-up area is 50 km/h. It applies whenever there are no signs saying otherwise, so you will not always see a sign confirming it.

text: You are on a rural road outside any built-up area and there are no speed limit signs. What is the maximum speed you may travel?
options: 80 km/h
90 km/h
100 km/h
110 km/h
explanation: The default limit outside built-up areas is 100 km/h. Roads signed at 110 km/h are the exception and are always signposted.

text: What does a speed limit sign actually tell you?
options: The average speed expected over the road
The speed you should aim to travel at
The maximum speed allowed in good conditions
The minimum safe speed for that road
explanation: A speed limit is a maximum, not a target. In rain, fog, heavy traffic or poor light the safe speed is lower, and you can still be charged for driving too fast for the conditions while under the posted limit.

text: What is the speed limit in a shared zone?
options: 10 km/h
20 km/h
30 km/h
40 km/h
explanation: A shared zone is 10 km/h. Pedestrians share the roadway with vehicles in a shared zone, and you must give way to them.

text: You are approaching a curve with a yellow advisory speed sign showing 45. What does it mean?
options: A legal speed limit of 45 km/h that you must not exceed
A recommended maximum for the curve in good conditions
The speed limit for heavy vehicles only
The minimum speed you must maintain through the curve
explanation: Yellow advisory signs recommend a safe speed for the hazard ahead; they are not enforceable limits on their own. The posted speed limit still applies, and in the wet you should be slower than the advisory speed.

text: You are passing a stationary emergency vehicle displaying flashing blue or red lights. What must you do?
options: Stop completely until the emergency vehicle moves off
Maintain the posted speed limit and stay in your lane
Sound your horn to acknowledge the crew
Slow to 40 km/h and give the vehicle and its crew a wide berth
explanation: You must slow to 40 km/h when passing a stationary emergency vehicle with flashing lights, and move over to give the crew room if it is safe to do so. Resume the normal limit once you are clear of the scene.

text: Roadworks signs show a reduced speed limit but you cannot see any workers. What speed applies?
options: The reduced limit shown on the roadworks signs
Whatever speed feels safe for the road surface
The normal limit, provided you drive carefully
The normal limit, because the workers have gone
explanation: Roadworks speed limits are legally enforceable and apply whether or not workers are present. Loose surfaces, changed line markings and equipment remain hazards after the crew has left.

text: How does braking distance change if you double your speed?
options: It roughly quadruples
It stays about the same
It roughly doubles
It roughly triples
explanation: Braking distance rises with the square of speed, so doubling your speed roughly quadruples the distance needed to stop. This is on top of the reaction distance travelled before you touch the brake.

text: What is the minimum following distance you should keep behind the vehicle in front in dry conditions?
options: Two seconds
Six seconds
Four seconds
One second
explanation: Two seconds is the minimum in good conditions. Pick a fixed object, and if you reach it before counting two seconds after the vehicle ahead passed it, you are too close. Double it to at least four seconds in rain or poor visibility.

text: It is raining heavily and the posted limit is 100 km/h. What speed should you drive?
options: Whatever speed keeps you with the traffic flow
Slower than 100 km/h, at a speed suited to the conditions
100 km/h, since that is the legal limit
Exactly 80 km/h, the standard wet weather limit
explanation: The posted limit applies to good conditions. In heavy rain, grip and visibility drop and stopping distances lengthen, so you must slow down. There is no separate posted wet-weather limit — the judgement is yours.

text: You pass a sign showing 80 in a red circle. Where does that limit end?
options: At the next speed limit sign showing a different limit
At the next intersection
When you leave the built-up area
After one kilometre
explanation: A speed limit continues until another speed limit sign changes it. Intersections, town boundaries and distance travelled do not end it by themselves.

text: You are in the right lane of a 90 km/h multi-lane road, travelling at 90 km/h. A driver behind is tailgating you. What should you do?
options: Brake sharply to warn them off
Move left when it is safe and let them pass
Speed up to put distance between you
Hold your speed and position, since you are at the limit
explanation: Move left and let them go. Keeping left when practical is the rule on multi-lane roads, and being deliberately in someone's way makes an aggressive driver more dangerous, not less. Never brake-check a tailgater.

text: Which of these has the greatest effect on how badly someone is injured if you hit them?
options: The colour of your vehicle
How new your vehicle is
The speed at impact
The time of day
explanation: Impact speed matters most, because the energy in a crash rises with the square of speed. A pedestrian hit at 50 km/h is far more likely to be killed than one hit at 30 km/h.

text: What is reaction distance?
options: The distance travelled while you see a hazard and move your foot to the brake
The gap you should leave behind another vehicle
The distance at which headlights let you see a hazard
The distance the car travels once the brakes are applied
explanation: Reaction distance is the ground covered between spotting a hazard and the brakes taking effect. At 60 km/h you cover about 17 metres per second, so even a sharp reaction uses up a car length or three before you slow at all.

text: You are driving at night on an unlit road with low beam headlights. How should you choose your speed?
options: By matching the vehicle in front
As fast as the road surface allows
So you can stop within the distance you can see to be clear
By the posted speed limit alone
explanation: Never drive faster than your stopping distance within the lit road ahead. Low beam typically shows 50 to 60 metres, which is less than the stopping distance at 100 km/h, so unlit rural roads at night often call for well under the posted limit.

text: A speed limit sign shows 40 with 'SCHOOL ZONE' and times below it. When does the 40 km/h limit apply?
options: All day, every day
Only when children are visible
Only during school terms, at any hour
During the signposted times on school days
explanation: The limit applies during the times shown on the sign, on school days, whether or not you can see any children. Children step out from between parked cars, so do not treat an empty footpath as the all-clear.

text: You are travelling downhill on a long, steep grade in a heavily loaded car. How should you control your speed?
options: Select a lower gear and use the brakes intermittently
Coast in neutral to save fuel
Ride the brakes continuously the whole way down
Switch off the engine and freewheel
explanation: A lower gear lets the engine do most of the braking. Continuous braking overheats the brakes and they fade; coasting in neutral or with the engine off removes engine braking and, in many cars, power steering.

text: Traffic around you is travelling at 70 km/h in a signed 60 km/h zone. What speed may you legally drive?
options: 65 km/h, allowing for speedometer error
Any speed, provided you keep up with traffic
Up to 60 km/h
70 km/h, to match the traffic flow
explanation: The posted limit binds you regardless of what other drivers are doing. Matching a speeding traffic flow is not a defence.

text: You are approaching a crest and cannot see the road beyond it. What should you do?
options: Move to the right to see further ahead
Ease off and be ready to stop for anything hidden beyond the crest
Accelerate to clear the crest quickly
Maintain speed, since the limit has not changed
explanation: A crest hides stopped vehicles, stock and oncoming traffic on your side of the road. Slow enough to stop within the distance you can actually see, and stay left — moving right puts you head-on with anything coming over.

text: What is the effect of driving on gravel at the same speed you would use on sealed road?
options: No difference, as long as the tyres are good
Grip is much lower, so braking and steering take far longer to take effect
Only braking is affected, not steering
Grip improves because the surface is rougher
explanation: Loose gravel cuts grip sharply. Braking, steering and accelerating all need more room, and sudden inputs can slide the car. Slow down before a corner on gravel, not during it.

text: You see a sign with a number in a blue circle. What is it telling you?
options: The maximum speed permitted
The speed limit for buses
A minimum speed you must maintain
An advisory speed for a curve
explanation: A number in a blue circle is a minimum speed sign — you must not drive slower than that speed unless conditions make it unsafe. Maximum limits are shown in a red circle.

text: You are following a heavy truck on a wet road. What following distance is appropriate?
options: The usual two seconds
One car length for every 10 km/h
At least four seconds
Less than two seconds, so you can see past it
explanation: Wet roads alone call for doubling the two-second gap. Behind a truck you also need the extra distance to see around it and to stay out of its spray, and the driver cannot see you at all if you sit close behind.

text: You arrive at an intersection with no signs, no traffic lights and no line markings, at the same time as a car on your right. Who goes first?
options: Whoever indicates first
You do, because you are on their left
The car on your right
Whoever arrived first
explanation: At an uncontrolled intersection you give way to any vehicle approaching from your right. Arriving first does not give you priority.

text: You are turning right at an uncontrolled intersection. An oncoming car is going straight ahead. Who gives way?
options: You give way to the oncoming car
The oncoming car, because you are turning
Neither, if you both have room to proceed
Whoever is travelling slower
explanation: A driver turning right gives way to oncoming vehicles going straight ahead or turning left. Turning across a stream of traffic never gives you priority over it.

text: What must you do at a STOP sign?
options: Stop only if another vehicle is approaching
Sound your horn and proceed
Stop completely at the stop line, then give way to all traffic
Slow down and proceed if the way is clear
explanation: A stop sign requires a complete stop at the stop line — wheels stationary — every time, even on an empty road. You then give way to all traffic and pedestrians before proceeding.

text: What must you do at a GIVE WAY sign?
options: Slow down, be ready to stop, and give way to traffic in or approaching the intersection
Come to a complete stop every time
Give way only to vehicles coming from your right
Proceed at normal speed if you can see it is clear
explanation: A give way sign requires you to slow and be prepared to stop, then give way to all traffic in or approaching the intersection. You must stop if that is what giving way requires.

text: You are at a T-junction, driving on the road that ends. There are no signs or lights. What must you do?
options: Proceed, since you arrived first
Give way only to vehicles on your right
Give way to all vehicles on the continuing road
Give way only to vehicles turning into your road
explanation: At a T-junction the driver on the terminating road gives way to all traffic on the continuing road, from both directions.

text: Traffic lights turn green as you approach, but a car is still stopped in the middle of the intersection. What should you do?
options: Wait until the intersection is clear before entering
Reverse to give them room
Sound your horn and drive around them
Proceed, since you have a green light
explanation: A green light means you may proceed only if the intersection is clear. You must not enter an intersection unless you can get through without being trapped in it.

text: The traffic light turns yellow as you approach. What should you do?
options: Stop if you can do so safely
Continue at the same speed, since yellow means caution
Accelerate to clear the intersection
Stop immediately regardless of what is behind you
explanation: Yellow means stop if you can do so safely. You may only continue through if stopping would require braking so hard that it is unsafe, such as when a vehicle is close behind.

text: You are turning left at traffic lights with a green light. Pedestrians are crossing the road you are turning into. What must you do?
options: Give way to the pedestrians
Sound your horn to warn them
Proceed, since your light is green
Give way only if they have started crossing
explanation: A green light does not override pedestrians. When turning at an intersection you must give way to pedestrians crossing the road you are entering.

text: You are leaving a driveway and crossing the footpath to enter the road. Who must you give way to?
options: Only traffic approaching from your right
Pedestrians on the footpath and all traffic on the road
Nobody, if you sound your horn first
Only vehicles on the road
explanation: Coming out of a driveway or property you give way to everything: pedestrians on the footpath first, then all vehicles on the road. Reverse out only when you cannot safely drive out forwards.

text: Traffic lights at an intersection have failed completely and are showing nothing. How should you treat the intersection?
options: Proceed as normal, since the lights are not working
Stop and wait for the lights to be repaired
Treat it as if each approach has a give way sign, and proceed with great care
As if it has no controls, giving way to the right
explanation: When lights fail, treat the intersection as uncontrolled and approach as though facing a give way sign: slow, be ready to stop, and only proceed when it is clearly safe. Other drivers may assume they have priority.

text: You are facing a red traffic light with a green right-turn arrow. What may you do?
options: Turn right or go straight ahead
Nothing, the red light overrides the arrow
Turn right or left
Turn right only, and only if the way is clear
explanation: A green arrow permits movement in that direction only. The red light still stops every other movement, so you may turn right but not go straight ahead or turn left.

text: An ambulance approaches with lights and siren while you are stopped at a red light in the left lane. What should you do?
options: Stay exactly where you are, since the light is red
Move out of its path if you can do so safely, even if that means crossing the stop line
Reverse away from the intersection
Drive through the red light immediately
explanation: You must give way to an emergency vehicle with lights or siren, and you are permitted to move out of its way when it is safe to do so. Move deliberately and only far enough to clear a path — do not panic across the intersection.

text: Both you and an oncoming vehicle are turning right at an intersection, passing each other. How should you pass?
options: Left side to left side, passing behind each other, unless signs or markings say otherwise
Whichever way is quicker
The larger vehicle turns first
Right side to right side, turning in front of each other
explanation: Two vehicles turning right pass in front of each other, keeping to the left of the centre of the intersection, unless road markings direct otherwise. This keeps both drivers' views of oncoming traffic open.

text: You are at a give way sign wanting to turn left. A cyclist is riding along the road you want to enter. What must you do?
options: Turn ahead of the cyclist, since bicycles are slower
Give way to the cyclist as you would to any vehicle
Give way only if the cyclist is in a bicycle lane
Sound your horn and proceed
explanation: A bicycle is a vehicle and has the same right of way as a car. Cyclists are easy to misjudge — they are often travelling faster than they look.

text: You want to make a U-turn at an intersection where it is permitted. Who must you give way to?
options: Nobody, since you are staying on the same road
Only traffic behind you
Only oncoming traffic
All other vehicles and pedestrians
explanation: A driver making a U-turn gives way to everyone: all vehicles from every direction and all pedestrians. A U-turn is the lowest priority manoeuvre on the road.

text: You are entering a road from a slip lane. What must you do?
options: Merge at whatever speed you are travelling
Stop completely before entering, every time
Expect traffic to make room for you
Give way to traffic already on the road you are entering
explanation: Traffic on the road you are joining has priority. Match your speed to the traffic and slot into a gap; if there is no gap, you must give way, and that can mean stopping at the end of the slip lane.

text: You approach a level crossing where the lights are flashing red but no train is in sight. What must you do?
options: Proceed slowly, since no train is visible
Cross only if a second vehicle waits with you
Stop and wait until the lights stop flashing
Stop, look both ways, then cross
explanation: Flashing red lights at a level crossing mean stop and stay stopped until they cease. Trains are far faster and quieter than they appear, and a second train may follow the first.

text: Traffic is banked up beyond an intersection and the light is green. What should you do?
options: Sound your horn at the queued traffic
Stay behind the stop line until you can clear the intersection
Enter the intersection and wait for the queue to move
Enter and turn left instead
explanation: You must not enter an intersection unless you can drive right through it. Stopping in the middle blocks the cross traffic when their light turns green, and it is an offence.

text: You are turning right from a road with a painted median strip into a side street. Traffic is heavy. What is the safest approach?
options: Wait in the median strip until the near lane is clear, if it is long enough to hold your car
Turn left instead and do a U-turn
Reverse back and try a different route
Cross both directions in one movement no matter what
explanation: Where a median is wide enough to hold your vehicle clear of both traffic streams, you may cross in two stages. Never commit to crossing the second stream until you can complete it — being stranded across a lane is how right-turn crashes happen.

text: A vehicle is doing a three-point turn across the road ahead of you and is blocking your lane. What should you do?
options: Reverse away
Slow down and wait for them to complete the turn
Overtake on the wrong side of the road
Sound your horn and squeeze past
explanation: Wait. The driver turning must give way to you, but forcing the issue while they are committed across the road achieves nothing except a collision.

text: You are on a narrow road where an obstruction blocks your side of the carriageway. An oncoming vehicle is approaching. Who gives way?
options: You do, because the obstruction is on your side
The oncoming vehicle, since you are already committed
Neither, both should proceed slowly
Whoever is closer to the obstruction
explanation: If the obstruction is on your side of the road, the oncoming vehicle has right of way. You must wait until the road is clear before passing the obstruction.

text: You are stopped at a red light intending to turn left. There is no 'left turn on red permitted after stopping' sign. May you turn?
options: Yes, after stopping and checking it is clear
No, you must wait for a green light or green arrow
Yes, provided you indicate first
Yes, if no pedestrians are present
explanation: Turning left on a red light is only permitted where a sign specifically allows it. Without that sign a red light means stop and wait.

text: Two vehicles arrive at a four-way intersection where all four approaches have stop signs. You are on the left of the other vehicle. Who proceeds first?
options: You do, because you are on the left
Whoever is going straight ahead
Whoever stopped first
The vehicle on your right
explanation: Once both drivers have obeyed their stop signs, the ordinary give way rules resume: you give way to the vehicle on your right.

text: You are approaching an intersection where you have right of way, but a vehicle on the side road shows no sign of slowing. What should you do?
options: Cover the brake, slow down and be ready to stop
Flash your headlights and continue
Sound your horn and continue
Maintain speed, since you have right of way
explanation: Right of way is something other drivers give you, not something that protects you. When a vehicle is not behaving as expected, slow down and keep the option of stopping.

text: You are turning right at traffic lights on a green light with no arrow. Where should you wait?
options: In the intersection, positioned to turn, giving way to oncoming traffic
Behind the stop line until the light turns yellow
On the far side of the intersection
In the left lane to keep the intersection clear
explanation: On a full green you may enter the intersection and wait to turn, giving way to oncoming traffic. Keep your wheels straight so you are not pushed into oncoming traffic if hit from behind, and complete the turn when a gap appears or as the lights change.

text: A police officer is directing traffic at an intersection and signals you to proceed, but the traffic light is red. What should you do?
options: Wait for the officer to turn the lights off
Follow the police officer's direction
Proceed only if other vehicles do
Obey the red light and wait
explanation: Directions from a police officer or authorised traffic controller override traffic lights and signs.

text: When entering a roundabout, who must you give way to?
options: Vehicles entering from the road opposite
Any vehicle already in the roundabout
Nobody, if you are going straight ahead
Vehicles approaching from your right only
explanation: You give way to any vehicle already in the roundabout. In practice most of those come from your right, but the rule is about vehicles already circulating, not about direction.

text: You are turning left at a multi-lane roundabout. Which lane should you use and what should you signal?
options: Either lane, signal left on exit only
Left lane, signal left on approach
Left lane, no signal needed
Right lane, signal left on approach
explanation: Turning left: approach in the left lane, signal left on approach, and keep signalling left as you leave.

text: You are turning right at a multi-lane roundabout. Which lane should you use and what should you signal?
options: Right lane, signal right on approach
Left lane, signal right on approach
Right lane, no signal on approach
Either lane, signal right on approach
explanation: Turning right: approach in the right lane and signal right. Once you pass the exit before the one you want, change your signal to left.

text: You are going straight ahead at a roundabout. What should you signal on approach?
options: Signal left
Signal right
Signal right, then left
No signal on approach, but signal left before exiting
explanation: Going straight ahead needs no approach signal. You must still signal left before leaving the roundabout, if it is practical to do so.

text: When must you signal left at a roundabout?
options: Never, roundabout exits do not require signals
Only when turning left
Only at multi-lane roundabouts
When leaving the roundabout, if it is practical to do so
explanation: You must signal left when leaving a roundabout whenever it is practical. At a very small roundabout there may not be time between exits, which is what 'practical' allows for.

text: You are in the left lane of a two-lane roundabout going straight ahead. A vehicle in the right lane starts to move left across your path towards the same exit. What should you do?
options: Sound the horn and maintain speed
Accelerate to get past them
Hold your line and your speed
Ease off and let them across, then continue
explanation: You are entitled to your lane, but yielding costs you a second and avoids a crash. Roundabout sideswipes happen exactly here, so keep watching the vehicle beside you all the way round.

text: May you make a U-turn at a roundabout?
options: Only where a sign specifically permits it
Yes, by continuing around and taking the exit you came from
No, never
Only at single-lane roundabouts
explanation: You may turn around at a roundabout by driving right around and leaving by the road you entered from. Approach in the right lane, signal right, and signal left after passing the last exit before yours.

text: A cyclist is riding around a multi-lane roundabout in the left lane and does not move to the right lane to turn right. Is this permitted?
options: Yes, a cyclist may turn right from the left lane of a roundabout
No, cyclists must follow the same lane rules as cars
Only on roundabouts with a bicycle lane
Only if the cyclist dismounts
explanation: Cyclists are allowed to stay in the left lane of a multi-lane roundabout and turn right from it. They must give way to any vehicle leaving the roundabout, and you should expect a cyclist on your left to keep circulating.

text: You are approaching a roundabout and can see it is completely clear. Must you stop?
options: No, but you must slow and be ready to give way
Yes, unless you are turning left
No, you may enter at the full speed limit
Yes, always stop at a roundabout
explanation: A roundabout is a give way situation, not a stop sign. If it is genuinely clear you may drive through, but you must approach at a speed that lets you give way if it is not.

text: A long vehicle in front of you is straddling both lanes as it goes around a roundabout. What should you do?
options: Pass it on the right at speed
Sound the horn to make it keep left
Stay well back and do not attempt to pass alongside it
Overtake it on the inside
explanation: Long vehicles need both lanes to get around and often display a 'Do Not Overtake Turning Vehicle' sign. The rear of the trailer sweeps across the inside lane, so anything beside it gets crushed.

text: You entered a roundabout intending to take the second exit but realise you should have taken the first. What should you do?
options: Continue to the next exit, or go around again
Cut across to the first exit immediately
Brake and reverse to the first exit
Stop in the roundabout and wait for a gap
explanation: Carry on. Cutting across an exit line, stopping or reversing in a roundabout puts you in front of traffic that is not expecting it. Going round a second time costs nothing.

text: Two vehicles arrive at a single-lane roundabout at the same moment, from opposite directions. Both are going straight ahead. What happens?
options: Neither is in the roundabout yet, so each gives way to the vehicle on their right
The faster vehicle goes first
Both must stop and wait
Both may proceed, since their paths do not cross
explanation: Going straight ahead from opposite directions, the two paths do not conflict — each vehicle passes through its own half. The give way rule matters where paths actually cross.

text: What does a roundabout sign with arrows and lane markings on the approach tell you?
options: The speed limit for the roundabout
Which lanes may be used for which exits
That the roundabout is controlled by traffic lights
The number of exits
explanation: Approach lane arrows and signs set which lane you must be in for the exit you want. They override the general left-lane / right-lane rule, so read them before you commit.

text: A pedestrian is crossing the road at the exit of a roundabout you are leaving. What must you do?
options: Proceed, since you are already in the roundabout
Sound your horn to move them along
Give way only if they are on a marked crossing
Give way to the pedestrian
explanation: Being in the roundabout does not give you priority over pedestrians on the road you are entering. Look at the exit before you take it, not just at the traffic beside you.

text: You are approaching a roundabout in the right lane intending to go straight ahead, and there are no lane arrows. Is this permitted?
options: Only if the left lane is occupied
Yes, you may use either lane to go straight ahead unless signs or markings say otherwise
No, straight-ahead traffic must use the left lane
Only at roundabouts with more than four exits
explanation: Without arrows or signs directing otherwise, you may go straight ahead from either lane. Leave from the lane that matches — from the right lane, exit into the right lane.

text: Traffic in a roundabout is queued and there is no room for your vehicle to clear the roundabout. What should you do?
options: Wait at the entry line until there is room to get through
Enter anyway to hold your place
Take the first exit instead
Enter and stop in the roundabout
explanation: Do not enter a roundabout unless you can get out of it. Stopping inside blocks every other approach.

text: When should you begin looking for a gap as you approach a roundabout?
options: As soon as you enter the roundabout
Once you have stopped at the entry line
While still approaching, scanning to your right as you slow
Only after the vehicle in front has entered
explanation: Scan to the right as you slow on approach. If the gap is there you keep rolling; if it is not, you are already at a speed where you can stop. Waiting until you have stopped to start looking holds up everyone behind.

text: A vehicle already in the roundabout is signalling left, indicating it will take the exit before yours. What should you do?
options: Enter and give way once inside
Wait until you can see it actually beginning to leave
Enter immediately, since it is leaving
Sound your horn to confirm its intention
explanation: A signal is an intention, not a guarantee. Drivers leave indicators on by mistake or change their minds. Wait until the vehicle's movement confirms it is leaving.

text: What is the correct road position when driving around a single-lane roundabout?
options: As wide as possible, near the outer edge
Following the curve of the roundabout, keeping in the lane
As close to the central island as possible
Cutting straight across the centre if it is a small roundabout
explanation: Follow the curve within the marked lane. Cutting across the central island of a small roundabout is an offence unless the island is a mountable one designed for long vehicles.

text: You are exiting a roundabout and a vehicle is waiting to enter from that exit road. Who has priority?
options: You do — they must give way to vehicles in the roundabout
Whoever moves first
The waiting vehicle, since you are leaving
Neither, both should stop
explanation: Vehicles entering give way to those already circulating. Signalling left as you leave tells the waiting driver they can go, which is why the exit signal matters.

text: An emergency vehicle with lights and siren approaches while you are in a roundabout. What should you do?
options: Stop immediately where you are
Reverse out of the roundabout
Speed up to get out of the way
Leave the roundabout at the next exit, then pull over and stop
explanation: Clear the roundabout first, then pull left and stop. Stopping inside the roundabout blocks the very path the emergency vehicle needs.

text: You are in the right lane of a two-lane roundabout and want to take an exit that only the left lane may use. What should you do?
options: Continue around and re-enter in the correct lane
Stop and wait for a gap in the left lane
Take the exit from the right lane, indicating early
Change lanes inside the roundabout and take the exit
explanation: Cutting across to an exit you are not positioned for is how roundabout collisions happen. Go around again and approach in the correct lane — the second lap is the cheap option.

text: How long before a turn must you signal?
options: Only if other vehicles are nearby
Immediately before you turn
Exactly three seconds
Long enough to give sufficient warning to other road users
explanation: The rule is sufficient warning, which depends on speed and traffic. At speed that means well before you slow down; in a car park it may be a moment. Signal even when you think nobody is watching.

text: How long must you signal before moving out from a parked position at the kerb?
options: Long enough to warn others, and you must check your blind spot
At least five seconds
Only when traffic is heavy
No signal is required
explanation: Signal for long enough to warn others, and check mirrors and blind spot before moving. Pulling out from the kerb means giving way to all traffic already on the road.

text: Where should you position your vehicle to turn left from a two-way road?
options: Wherever gives the smoothest line
Toward the centre line to swing wide
In the centre of your lane, well out from the kerb
As near as practical to the left side of the road
explanation: Turn left from as near as practical to the left. Swinging out to the right first invites a vehicle or cyclist up your left side, which is exactly where you are about to turn.

text: Where should you position your vehicle to turn right from a two-way road?
options: Anywhere in your lane
In the middle of the road, just left of the centre line
On the right-hand side of the centre line
As near as practical to the left side
explanation: Move as close as practical to the centre of the road, staying on your own side of the centre line. This lets traffic behind pass on your left while you wait for a gap.

text: You are waiting to turn right and have stopped in the intersection with your wheels turned to the right. Why is this dangerous?
options: It blocks the view of drivers behind
It wears out the steering
It is not dangerous, it saves time
If you are struck from behind you will be pushed into oncoming traffic
explanation: Keep the wheels straight until you actually begin the turn. With them turned, a rear-end shunt pushes you head-on into the oncoming stream.

text: When may you make a U-turn?
options: Only at intersections with traffic lights
Where you have a clear view of approaching traffic and no sign prohibits it
Only on roads with a speed limit of 60 km/h or less
Anywhere, as long as it is safe
explanation: A U-turn needs a clear view of approaching traffic in both directions, no prohibiting sign, and no unbroken centre line unless a break allows it. You must give way to everyone.

text: When should you check your blind spot before changing lanes?
options: Only on motorways
After signalling and checking mirrors, immediately before moving
Blind spot checks are unnecessary with modern mirrors
Before signalling
explanation: Mirror, signal, mirror, head check, then move. The head check comes last because a motorcyclist or cyclist can arrive in the blind spot in the time between your first mirror check and the move.

text: You are turning left and a bicycle rider is travelling straight ahead in a bicycle lane on your left. What must you do?
options: Speed up to complete the turn first
Turn ahead of the cyclist
Sound your horn and turn
Give way to the cyclist before crossing the bicycle lane
explanation: Crossing a bicycle lane to turn left means giving way to any cyclist in it. Turning across a rider on your inside is one of the most common ways cyclists are hurt.

text: You are in a right-turn lane and change your mind, wanting to go straight ahead. What should you do?
options: Go straight ahead from the turning lane
Move across into the through lane before the intersection
Complete the right turn and find another route
Stop and wait for a gap to move across
explanation: Once you are in a turn lane you must go that way. Cutting across at the last moment is both illegal and unexpected by everyone around you.

text: You are turning right into a road with two lanes in your direction. Which lane should you turn into?
options: The right lane always
Either lane, unless signs or markings direct otherwise
The left lane always
Whichever lane has less traffic
explanation: You may turn into either lane unless markings say otherwise, but you must not cross lanes mid-turn. Choose before you start and hold that line.

text: When must you turn off your indicator?
options: As soon as the manoeuvre is complete
When the next vehicle passes
After ten seconds
It cancels automatically, so you never need to
explanation: Cancel it once the manoeuvre is done. Self-cancelling only works on a sharp enough turn, and an indicator left on tells everyone you are about to do something you are not.

text: You are behind a long vehicle displaying a 'Do Not Overtake Turning Vehicle' sign, and it is signalling left but has swung out to the right. What should you do?
options: Stay behind it until the turn is complete
Pass on its left, since it has moved right
Pass on its right
Sound your horn to tell it to keep left
explanation: Long vehicles must swing wide to get around a corner, and the trailer cuts back across the space it just left. That sign makes it an offence to pass on either side while it is turning.

text: What is the correct sequence before changing lanes?
options: Check blind spot, move, then signal
Signal, move, then check mirrors
Move first, signal if another driver reacts
Check mirrors, signal, check blind spot, then move if clear
explanation: Mirrors first so you know what is around you, then signal to give others warning, then a head check for the blind spot, then move. Signalling is a warning, not a right to move.

text: You need to reverse out of a driveway into a busy street. What is the safest approach?
options: Ask a passenger to stand in the road and stop traffic
Reverse out slowly with the radio off
Reverse out quickly to spend less time in the road
Drive in forwards when you arrive so you can drive out forwards
explanation: Reversing into a road gives you the worst possible view of traffic and pedestrians. Where you can, reverse into the driveway on arrival so you leave facing out.

text: You are making a hook turn at an intersection where one is required. Where do you wait?
options: On the far side of the intersection
In the right lane, as for a normal right turn
In the far left of the intersection, until the lights on the road you are entering turn green
Behind the stop line in the left lane
explanation: A hook turn is made from the left: you pull forward to the far left of the intersection and wait, then complete the right turn when the lights on the road you are entering go green. Signs mark the intersections where it applies.

text: A car ahead is signalling left but has not slowed down and is nowhere near a side street. What should you assume?
options: The indicator may have been left on by mistake — wait for the vehicle's behaviour to confirm it
The driver wants you to overtake
It will turn left immediately
The vehicle has a fault and will stop
explanation: Judge other drivers by what the vehicle is doing, not by what its lights claim. Confirm with speed and road position before you act on someone else's signal.

text: You are turning right across an oncoming lane and a large vehicle in that lane blocks your view of the traffic behind it. What should you do?
options: Turn quickly while the large vehicle screens you
Wait until you can see clearly past it before turning
Edge out slowly into the oncoming lane to see
Turn if the large vehicle flashes its lights at you
explanation: A gap you cannot see into is not a gap. Motorcycles and cars overtaking a slow vehicle come through exactly that blind space. Wait for a clear view, even if a driver waves you on.

text: Where must you not make a U-turn?
options: Anywhere on a two-lane road
Anywhere a bus route operates
Across an unbroken centre line, or where a No U-turn sign applies
Anywhere within a built-up area
explanation: You may not U-turn across an unbroken (continuous) centre line, or where a No U-turn sign is displayed, or at traffic lights unless a sign permits it.

text: You are merging where your lane ends and there are no lane lines marked. Who must give way?
options: Whichever vehicle is travelling faster
You must give way to any vehicle whose front is ahead of yours
The vehicle behind always gives way
The vehicle in the ending lane gives way
explanation: Where lines end and lanes merge, the rule is 'zip': give way to any vehicle already ahead of you. Match speed and blend into the gap rather than racing to the front.

text: You are changing lanes where the lanes are separated by a broken white line. Who must give way?
options: Neither vehicle
The vehicle already in the lane you are moving into
You must give way to traffic already in that lane
Whichever vehicle is behind
explanation: Moving from a marked lane into another means giving way to anything already there. A gap that requires the other driver to brake was not a gap.

text: Why should you avoid braking hard while already turning a corner?
options: It wears the brake pads unevenly
It is illegal to brake mid-corner
It uses more fuel
The tyres are already using grip to steer, so braking can break traction
explanation: A tyre has a fixed budget of grip and cornering is already spending it. Do your braking in a straight line before the corner, then steer through it on a light, steady throttle.

text: You are turning left out of a side street into a road where traffic is heavy. A driver on the main road flashes their headlights at you. What does that mean legally?
options: It is a legal signal that you may proceed
It means they are about to turn
It has no legal meaning — you must still judge for yourself that it is safe
It is a warning that you must wait
explanation: A flash of headlights carries no legal weight and only tells you about one driver. The vehicle in the next lane, or a motorcycle filtering past, has told you nothing. Judge the gap yourself.

text: What shape and colour is a STOP sign?
options: Yellow diamond with black lettering
Red triangle pointing down
Red octagon with white lettering
White circle with a red border
explanation: A stop sign is a red octagon — the only eight-sided sign on the road, so it is recognisable even when dirty or seen from an angle.

text: What do yellow diamond-shaped signs tell you?
options: Information about services and destinations
A temporary roadworks condition
A legal instruction you must obey
A warning about a hazard or a change in road conditions ahead
explanation: Yellow diamonds are warnings: a curve, a crest, an intersection, livestock, a change in the road. They tell you what to expect so you can adjust before you get there.

text: What does a red circle or red border on a sign generally indicate?
options: A warning of a hazard
Information
A prohibition or a limit you must obey
A tourist route
explanation: Red on a regulatory sign means a restriction: a speed limit, no entry, no right turn, no parking. Disobeying it is an offence.

text: What does an orange or yellow-orange diamond sign indicate?
options: A tourist attraction
Roadworks or a temporary condition ahead
A permanent hazard
A school zone
explanation: Orange signs mark roadworks and temporary conditions — loose gravel, workers ahead, changed traffic conditions. Any speed limit posted with them is legally enforceable.

text: You see a sign showing a black cross on a yellow diamond, with a second sign showing crossed rails. What is ahead?
options: A crossroads intersection
A pedestrian crossing
A railway level crossing
A hospital
explanation: That is a level crossing. Slow, look both ways, and be ready to stop — never queue onto the tracks, and never start crossing unless you can clear the far side.

text: What does a white sign with a red circle and a red diagonal line through a symbol mean?
options: That activity is prohibited here
That activity is permitted here
The sign is advisory only
That activity is recommended
explanation: A red circle with a diagonal stroke prohibits whatever is shown inside it — no U-turn, no parking, no trucks.

text: A sign shows a picture of two children walking. What does it mean?
options: A playground is nearby
Children are not permitted on this road
Watch for children — a school or children's crossing area ahead
A childcare centre is for sale
explanation: It warns you to expect children near the road. Children move unpredictably and are short enough to be hidden by parked cars, so slow down and cover the brake.

text: What does a sign showing a large arrow curving to the left on a black and white chevron pattern mean?
options: Overtaking lane ahead
The road ends ahead
Left lane closed
A sharp change of direction — the road turns sharply left here
explanation: Chevron alignment markers mark a sharp change of direction. Several in a row show the severity of the bend. Slow before you reach them, not in the middle of them.

text: What does a NO ENTRY sign mean?
options: You must not drive past this sign in that direction
Entry is restricted to local traffic
Entry permitted outside business hours
Enter with caution
explanation: No entry means exactly that. It usually marks a one-way street from the wrong end, so driving past it puts you head-on into traffic.

text: A sign shows the letter 'T' as a symbol. What does it mean?
options: Toll road ahead
Truck route
Tourist route
The road ahead ends in a T-junction
explanation: A T symbol on a yellow diamond warns that the road ends in a T-junction. You will have to turn left or right and give way to the road you are joining.

text: What does a blue and white 'P' sign with times listed underneath mean?
options: Parking is permitted, subject to the conditions and times shown
Parking is banned during those times
Passenger drop-off only
Police patrol during those hours
explanation: A blue-and-white P sign permits parking under the stated conditions, such as '2P 8am-6pm' meaning a two-hour limit in those hours. A red-and-white sign prohibits instead.

text: You see a yellow diamond sign showing a car with wavy lines under it. What is it warning about?
options: A car wash
Speed humps
A slippery surface
A water crossing ahead
explanation: The skidding-car symbol warns of a slippery surface. Reduce speed and avoid harsh braking, steering or acceleration over that stretch.

text: What does a sign showing a kangaroo or wombat symbol on a yellow diamond mean?
options: A wildlife park is nearby
Wildlife may be on the road, especially at dawn and dusk
Feeding wildlife is permitted
This is a wildlife sanctuary boundary
explanation: Animals cross here. In Tasmania this is a serious risk on rural roads at dawn, dusk and night. Brake in a straight line rather than swerving — swerving for an animal has killed drivers.

text: What does a KEEP LEFT sign on an island in the road mean?
options: You must pass to the left of the island
Left turn only
Keep left unless overtaking
The left lane is closed
explanation: It directs you around a specific obstruction — a traffic island or median — on the left side. It is a physical instruction about that island, not a general lane rule.

text: A green sign with white lettering shows place names and distances. What kind of sign is it?
options: A regulatory sign you must obey
A direction or information sign
A warning sign
A tourist attraction sign
explanation: Green signs give directions and distances on main routes. Read them early — deciding your exit at the last second causes far more trouble than missing it.

text: What does a sign reading 'ROAD SUBJECT TO FLOODING' with a depth indicator mean you should do when water is across the road?
options: Drive through quickly to create a bow wave
Drive through slowly in a low gear
Follow the vehicle in front through
Do not enter the water unless you are certain of its depth and the road beneath
explanation: Floodwater hides washouts and moves faster than it looks. A small depth of moving water floats a car. If you cannot see the road surface and be sure of the depth, turn around.

text: What does a sign showing a truck on a steep downward slope mean?
options: Truck parking area
A steep descent ahead — select a low gear
Trucks must stop
Trucks prohibited
explanation: A steep descent is ahead. Choose a lower gear before the hill so engine braking controls your speed and the brakes stay cool.

text: What does the sign 'GIVE WAY TO BUSES' mean?
options: Overtaking buses is prohibited
Always stop when you see a bus
You must give way to a bus signalling to pull out from a bus stop, in a signposted area
Buses may use any lane
explanation: In signposted areas you must give way to a bus signalling to move out from the kerb. The bus driver still has to move out safely.

text: What does a sign showing a bicycle in a white circle with a red border mean?
options: Watch for cyclists
Bicycle parking ahead
A bicycle lane begins
Bicycles are prohibited on this road
explanation: A symbol in a red-bordered circle prohibits it. A bicycle lane is marked in green or with a blue sign instead.

text: You see a rectangular white sign reading 'CLEARWAY' with times. What does it mean?
options: The road is closed during those times
You must not stop or park on that length of road during those times
Overtaking is permitted during those times
The road is clear of hazards during those times
explanation: A clearway bans stopping during the stated hours, even briefly to drop someone off. Vehicles left in a clearway are usually towed.

text: What does a yellow diamond sign showing a merging arrow mean?
options: A slip lane is ahead
An overtaking lane begins
A lane is ending and traffic must merge ahead
Two roads cross ahead
explanation: A lane ends ahead and traffic must merge. Adjust your speed and position early to make a gap rather than arriving at the merge point alongside another vehicle.

text: A sign shows a black circle with a diagonal black line on a white background. What does it mean?
options: The end of the restriction that was previously signposted
No stopping
No entry for all vehicles
A rest area ahead
explanation: The struck-through symbol ends the restriction it repeats — for example the end of an overtaking lane or a special limit. The default rules for that road resume.

text: Which of these signs must you obey even if you believe it is unnecessary?
options: Only warning signs
Only signs at intersections
All regulatory signs, such as stop, give way, speed limit and no entry
Only signs with times listed
explanation: Regulatory signs carry the force of law regardless of your judgement about the traffic. Warning and advisory signs advise; regulatory signs bind.

text: You approach a sign showing a red circle around the numbers '2.5m'. What does it tell you?
options: The distance to the next hazard
The road is 2.5 metres wide
A width or height limit that your vehicle must not exceed
The minimum following distance
explanation: A dimension inside a red circle is a physical limit for the structure ahead — a low bridge or narrow passage. Know your vehicle's height when towing or carrying a roof load.

text: What does a single unbroken (continuous) white line down the centre of the road mean?
options: You may cross it to overtake if the road is clear
It separates traffic travelling in the same direction
You must not cross it, except to enter or leave the road
It marks the edge of the road
explanation: You must not cross a continuous centre line, except to enter or leave a property or road, or to pass an obstruction where it is safe. It is placed where visibility is too poor to overtake.

text: What does a broken centre line mean?
options: You may cross it to overtake or turn when it is safe
It marks a bicycle lane
You must never cross it
It marks the edge of the sealed surface
explanation: A broken line may be crossed when it is safe — to overtake, turn, or pass an obstruction. Safe still means you can see far enough ahead and return without cutting anyone off.

text: There are two lines down the centre: a continuous line on your side and a broken line on the other. May you overtake?
options: Only if you can complete the overtake within 100 metres
Only if the oncoming lane is empty
Yes, because one line is broken
No — the line nearest you is continuous, so you must not cross
explanation: The line closest to you governs your movement. Continuous on your side means you stay put, even though traffic coming the other way may legally cross.

text: What do two continuous parallel lines down the centre of the road mean?
options: A wide road with room to overtake
Neither direction may cross the lines
A tram or bus lane
Overtaking permitted from both directions
explanation: Double continuous lines mean no crossing from either direction, except to enter or leave a property or road, or to pass an obstruction where it is safe.

text: What is a painted island — an area marked with diagonal stripes between lanes?
options: A bicycle storage area
An overtaking lane
An area you should not drive on, used to separate traffic streams
A parking area
explanation: Painted islands separate traffic and protect turning lanes. You should not drive on one, though you may drive across a painted island to enter a turning lane where it is legal and safe.

text: What do the parallel white stripes across a road at an intersection mean?
options: A pedestrian crossing where you must give way to pedestrians on it
A speed hump
A bicycle crossing only
A place where you may park
explanation: Broad white stripes mark a pedestrian crossing. You must give way to any pedestrian on the crossing or about to step onto it, and you must not overtake a vehicle stopped at one.

text: What does a continuous yellow line along the edge of the road mean?
options: Parking is permitted
A bus lane
A bicycle lane
No stopping at any time along that length of road
explanation: A continuous yellow edge line means no stopping at all on that length of road — not even briefly.

text: What is the white line across your lane at an intersection called, and what must you do at it?
options: A lane line — you may cross it freely
A stop line — stop behind it at a stop sign or red light
An edge line — it marks the road boundary
A give way line — you may drive over it at any time
explanation: The stop line marks where you must stop at a red light or stop sign. Stop behind it, not on it — it is placed to keep you clear of the cross traffic's path.

text: What does a broken line with the word 'GIVE WAY' or a triangle marked on the road mean?
options: You must stop completely
You must give way to traffic on the road you are entering
Parking is prohibited
You have right of way
explanation: A dotted give way line marks where you must give way. You need not stop if the way is clear, but you must slow enough to be able to.

text: What does a green painted section of road with a bicycle symbol indicate?
options: A bicycle parking area
A bicycle lane, which motor vehicles must generally keep out of
A section of road that is slippery
A pedestrian zone
explanation: Green paint marks a bicycle lane, usually where it crosses a conflict point. Motor vehicles must keep out of a bicycle lane except for the short distance needed to enter or leave the road or a parking space.

text: What does a continuous white line at the left-hand edge of the road mark?
options: The centre of the road
The edge of the traffic lane and the limit of the sealed surface
A bicycle lane
A no-stopping zone
explanation: An edge line marks the boundary of the traffic lane. In fog or heavy rain it is the most reliable reference you have — following the left edge line keeps you out of oncoming traffic.

text: You want to turn right into a driveway but there is a continuous centre line. May you cross it?
options: Only if you signal for at least five seconds
No, never cross a continuous line
Yes — crossing to enter or leave a property is permitted when safe
Only if there is a break in the line within 20 metres
explanation: Entering or leaving a property or road is one of the permitted reasons to cross a continuous line. It must still be safe, and you must give way to oncoming traffic.

text: What do the arrows painted in a lane at an intersection tell you?
options: The direction of the one-way street
Where to stop for the traffic lights
The only movements permitted from that lane
Suggested directions to popular destinations
explanation: A lane arrow restricts that lane to the movements shown. A left arrow alone means you must turn left from that lane, even if the lane ahead looks clear.

text: What does a zig-zag line painted on the road approaching a pedestrian crossing mean?
options: The road surface is uneven
You are approaching a crossing — do not overtake or park in that area
Cyclists must give way
The lane is about to end
explanation: Zig-zag markings warn of a crossing ahead and mark the zone where stopping, parking and overtaking are prohibited, so that a stopped vehicle never hides a pedestrian.

text: A broken line separates lanes travelling in the same direction. What does it mean?
options: You must never change lanes
The road is one-way
You may change lanes when it is safe to do so
Overtaking is prohibited
explanation: Broken lane lines may be crossed to change lanes when safe. You must give way to traffic already in the lane you are entering.

text: A continuous white line separates two lanes going in the same direction. What does it mean?
options: You are approaching a roundabout
The lane to the right is for buses
You should not change lanes across it
You may change lanes freely
explanation: A continuous line between same-direction lanes marks a place where changing lanes is unsafe — usually approaching an intersection or a merge. Stay in your lane until it becomes broken again.

text: What does the word 'KEEP CLEAR' painted in a box on the road mean?
options: Park only in this box
Only buses may use this area
Pedestrians may cross here
Do not stop in the box, even in queued traffic
explanation: A KEEP CLEAR box protects an access point — a driveway, a side street, an emergency exit. Do not enter it unless you can drive straight through.

text: You are on a road with a continuous centre line and a cyclist is riding slowly ahead of you. What may you do?
options: Sound your horn until the cyclist moves aside
Overtake within your own lane at any distance
Wait behind until the line becomes broken or the road widens
Cross the continuous line to overtake
explanation: You must leave a safe lateral distance when passing a cyclist — typically at least one metre at low speeds and more at higher speeds. If your lane does not allow that without crossing a continuous line, wait.

text: You are approaching an intersection and the lane lines become continuous. What does this tell you?
options: You should already be in the lane you need — stay in it through the intersection
You may now overtake
The road is about to become one-way
The speed limit is about to change
explanation: Continuous lane lines near an intersection mean the lane choice is made. Change lanes well before they start, not by cutting across at the stop line.

text: Fog has reduced visibility badly on an unfamiliar road. Which marking is safest to steer by?
options: The left edge line
The tail lights of the vehicle ahead
The centre line, to stay clear of the verge
The right edge of the road
explanation: Follow the left edge line. Steering by the centre line drifts you towards oncoming traffic, and following tail lights means you are matched to a driver who may be about to stop.

text: What is the minimum distance you should leave when passing a cyclist at 60 km/h or less?
options: 2 metres
0.5 metres
1 metre
No minimum applies
explanation: At 60 km/h or less you must leave at least one metre. Above 60 km/h it is at least 1.5 metres. If you cannot give that room, wait.

text: What is the minimum distance you should leave when passing a cyclist at more than 60 km/h?
options: 3 metres
1 metre
The width of your vehicle
1.5 metres
explanation: Above 60 km/h the minimum is 1.5 metres. At speed the air pressure from a passing vehicle alone can unbalance a rider.

text: A pedestrian is waiting at the kerb at a marked pedestrian crossing. What must you do?
options: Give way only if they are elderly or a child
Slow and be ready to stop, and give way to them as they enter the crossing
Sound your horn to let them know you are coming
Continue, since they have not stepped out yet
explanation: You must give way to a pedestrian on the crossing or about to step onto it. Approach at a speed that lets you stop, and never overtake a vehicle that has stopped at a crossing.

text: Why should you not sit close behind a heavy truck?
options: It is illegal to follow a truck
The truck will slow down
The truck driver cannot see you, and you cannot see the road ahead
It uses more fuel
explanation: Trucks have large blind spots directly behind and along both sides. If you cannot see the driver's mirrors, the driver cannot see you — and you lose your own view of what is happening in front of the truck.

text: You have just overtaken a heavy truck on a highway. When should you move back into the left lane?
options: Once you can see the whole truck in your rear-view mirror
Immediately after passing the cab
After 100 metres regardless of position
When the truck flashes its lights
explanation: Wait until the entire truck is visible in your interior mirror. Cutting in early leaves the truck no stopping distance, and a loaded truck needs far more room to stop than a car.

text: You are on a suburban street in a signposted 'give way to buses' area. A bus at a bus stop ahead switches on its right indicator to pull out. What must you do?
options: Sound your horn to tell the bus to wait
Stop completely and wait until the bus is out of sight
Give way to the bus, allowing it to move out from the stop
Continue at the same speed — buses always give way to through traffic
explanation: In signposted areas, a bus signalling to move out from a bus stop must be given way to. The rule applies on lower-speed roads; the bus driver must still pull out safely, so watch that they have seen you.

text: You are about to open your car door after parking on a busy street. What must you do?
options: Open it fully and step out
Open it quickly to spend less time exposed
Nothing — approaching traffic must avoid your door
Check mirrors and over your shoulder for cyclists and traffic before opening
explanation: Opening a door into the path of a cyclist is an offence and a common cause of serious injury. Check the mirror and look over your shoulder before you touch the handle.

text: Where may a cyclist legally ride on the road?
options: Only on the shoulder
Only in a bicycle lane
Only where there is no footpath
In a traffic lane, and two abreast is permitted
explanation: Cyclists may use a traffic lane and may ride two abreast, no more than 1.5 metres apart. They are entitled to the lane, and to move out from the kerb to avoid drains, debris and car doors.

text: Why are motorcycles easy to miss at intersections?
options: Their narrow profile is easily hidden by pillars, mirrors and other vehicles, and their speed is hard to judge
They usually travel faster than the speed limit
They rarely use headlights
They are quieter than cars
explanation: A motorcycle presents a narrow target that hides behind an A-pillar or another car, and its closing speed is genuinely hard to judge. Look twice for motorcycles before pulling out, and move your head to see around pillars.

text: A person using a mobility scooter is crossing the road ahead. How should you treat them?
options: As a cyclist
As a vehicle, which must give way to you
As a pedestrian, giving way as you would to a person on foot
As an obstruction to drive around
explanation: Motorised wheelchairs and mobility scooters are treated as pedestrians. They move slowly and may not be able to stop or change direction quickly, so give them room and time.

text: You are on a rural road and see livestock being moved along it. What should you do?
options: Sound your horn to move them along
Slow right down, or stop, and follow any direction from the person in charge
Overtake quickly on the right
Drive through the mob at low speed
explanation: Slow down or stop and let the animals settle. Horns and engine noise scatter stock, which is more dangerous for you than waiting. Follow the drover's directions.

text: A truck is turning left at an intersection and has swung out towards the centre of the road. What is the danger of moving up its left side?
options: There is no danger if you stay in your lane
The truck may drop its load
The trailer cuts back across the inside of the turn and can crush a vehicle beside it
The truck may reverse
explanation: A long vehicle's rear wheels track well inside the front, so the trailer sweeps across the space beside the cab. Never move into the gap a turning truck leaves on its inside.

text: You see a bus stopped ahead with children getting off. What should you do?
options: Sound your horn as you pass
Maintain speed and pass in the other lane
Slow down and be ready to stop — children may run out from in front of or behind the bus
Stop only if a school crossing flag is displayed
explanation: Children step out from in front of and behind buses without looking. Slow right down and cover the brake until you are well past.

text: What must you do when approaching a person with a white cane or a guide dog at the kerb?
options: Sound your horn to alert them
Continue, as they will wait for you
Flash your headlights
Give way and allow them to cross — they may not be able to see or hear your vehicle
explanation: A white cane or guide dog indicates a person who is blind or has low vision. They cannot judge your approach visually and a modern car may be nearly silent, so give way and let them cross.

text: You are in slow traffic and a motorcycle rides between the lanes past you. What should you do?
options: Sound your horn
Move over to block the gap
Hold your lane position steadily and check mirrors before any lane change
Speed up to close the gap
explanation: Hold your line and check mirrors and blind spot before any lane change in slow traffic. Deliberately closing a gap on a rider is dangerous and pointless.

text: Why do heavy vehicles need much longer to stop than cars?
options: They always travel faster
Drivers react more slowly
Their brakes are less effective by design
Their far greater mass takes much more distance to bring to a stop
explanation: A loaded truck can weigh thirty times what a car weighs, and all that momentum has to be shed through the tyres. A fully loaded truck at highway speed can need double a car's stopping distance or more.

text: A pedestrian steps onto the road mid-block, away from any crossing. What should you do?
options: Maintain speed, since they are crossing illegally
Swerve into the oncoming lane
Sound your horn and continue
Slow down and avoid them — you must not hit a pedestrian regardless of who has right of way
explanation: Right of way is no defence for hitting someone. Slow down, be prepared to stop, and give them room. Swerving into the oncoming lane trades one collision for a worse one.

text: May you drive in a bus lane?
options: Yes, at any time
No, except for the short distance needed to enter or leave the road or turn, where permitted
Yes, if you are carrying passengers
Yes, outside peak hours only
explanation: Bus lanes are for buses and any other vehicles named on the sign. Other traffic may only use them for the short distance needed to enter or leave the road or a parking space, where that is permitted.

text: A cyclist ahead of you moves out from the kerb towards the middle of the lane. What is the most likely reason?
options: They are lost
They want you to overtake
They are about to turn right
They are avoiding a hazard such as a drain, debris or a parked car's door zone
explanation: Riders move out to avoid drains, glass, potholes and the door zone of parked cars — hazards you may not be able to see. Give them room rather than assuming they have drifted.

text: You are driving past a row of parked cars in a residential street. What is the main hazard?
options: Losing traction on the road markings
Parked cars reversing without warning only
Paint damage from close passing
A pedestrian, child or cyclist emerging from between the vehicles, and doors opening
explanation: Parked cars hide people, particularly children, and their doors open without warning. Move out where you can, drop your speed, and watch under the parked cars for feet.

text: An emergency vehicle with lights and siren is approaching from behind on a single-lane road. What should you do?
options: Move left and stop when it is safe, giving it a clear path
Continue at the same speed and let it find a way past
Stop immediately where you are
Speed up to keep ahead of it
explanation: Move left and stop when it is safe. Stopping dead in the middle of the lane, or accelerating away, both leave the emergency vehicle nowhere to go.

text: You are following a vehicle towing a caravan on a winding road. What is the safest approach to overtaking?
options: Overtake as soon as any gap appears
Wait for an overtaking lane or a long clear straight — the combined length takes far longer to pass
Overtake on the left where the road is wider
Follow closely so you can accelerate past quickly
explanation: A car and caravan can be fifteen metres or more, so passing takes much longer than passing a car. Sit well back for a better view and wait for an overtaking lane or a genuinely long straight.

text: A vehicle displaying a large 'OVERSIZE' sign with a pilot vehicle is approaching on a narrow rural road. What should you do?
options: Sound your horn and continue
Maintain your speed and lane position
Overtake the pilot vehicle quickly
Slow down, move as far left as safely possible, and stop if directed by the pilot vehicle
explanation: Oversize loads can occupy more than their own lane. The pilot vehicle warns you and may direct you to slow or pull over — follow its instructions.

text: You are turning right and a pedestrian starts crossing the road you are turning into, against the pedestrian signal. What must you do?
options: Sound your horn and continue turning
Proceed, since they are crossing against the signal
Turn behind them at speed
Give way to them and wait until they have cleared your path
explanation: Whether or not the pedestrian is in the right, you must not drive into them. Give way, let them clear, and complete the turn afterwards.

text: What blood alcohol concentration must a learner driver in Tasmania not exceed?
explanation: Learner and provisional drivers must have a blood alcohol concentration of zero. Any alcohol at all in your system while driving on an L or P licence is an offence.

text: What is the general blood alcohol limit for a fully licensed driver in Australia?
explanation: Fully licensed drivers must stay under 0.05. Learners, provisional drivers and drivers of some commercial vehicles must be at zero.

text: Which of these will reliably lower your blood alcohol concentration before driving?
options: Eating a large meal
Drinking strong coffee
Having a cold shower
Time — nothing else speeds up how fast your body clears alcohol
explanation: Only time removes alcohol from your blood, at roughly one standard drink per hour. Coffee, food and a shower may make you feel more alert while leaving you just as impaired and just as illegal.

text: How does alcohol affect your driving even at low levels?
options: It improves confidence, which makes you safer
It slows reaction time, impairs judgement and reduces your ability to divide attention
It has no effect below 0.05
It only affects vision
explanation: Alcohol slows reactions, blurs judgement of speed and distance, and narrows attention — while making you feel more capable, not less. That gap between feeling fine and being impaired is what makes it so dangerous.

text: You have been prescribed medication that carries a warning about drowsiness. What should you do?
options: Drive only at night
Drive as normal, since it is prescribed
Take a smaller dose and drive
Check with your doctor or pharmacist whether it is safe to drive, and do not drive if it affects you
explanation: Prescription and over-the-counter medicines can impair driving as much as alcohol. A lawful prescription is not a defence for driving while impaired — ask before you drive.

text: What are the early warning signs of driver fatigue?
options: Wanting to drive faster
Feeling hungry
Yawning, heavy eyelids, drifting in the lane, and not remembering the last few kilometres
Increased alertness and faster reactions
explanation: Yawning, sore eyes, drifting, missed signs and blank patches of memory all say you are already impaired. By the time you notice them you have lost meaningful reaction time.

text: You start feeling drowsy on a long drive. What is the only reliable remedy?
options: Talking to a passenger
Opening the window and turning up the radio
Drinking an energy drink and continuing
Stopping somewhere safe and sleeping
explanation: Sleep is the only thing that fixes fatigue. Fresh air, loud music and caffeine buy a few minutes at best and mask how impaired you are. Pull over somewhere safe and rest — a 15 minute nap is worth more than any of them.

text: What is 'microsleep'?
options: A short nap taken deliberately at a rest stop
The first stage of falling asleep at night
A brief involuntary lapse into sleep of a few seconds, often without realising it
The drowsiness felt after a meal
explanation: A microsleep is an involuntary few seconds of sleep you may not even notice. At 100 km/h, four seconds covers more than 100 metres of road with nobody driving.

text: When is the risk of fatigue-related crashes highest?
options: Mid-morning
On weekends only
Late at night, early morning, and the early afternoon dip
During peak hour only
explanation: Your body clock pushes hardest towards sleep between about 2am and 6am, and again in the early afternoon. Plan long drives to avoid those windows.

text: How often should you take a break on a long drive?
options: At least every two hours
Breaks are unnecessary if you slept well
Only when you feel tired
Every four hours
explanation: Take a proper break at least every two hours — get out and move, not just stop. Waiting until you feel tired means waiting until you are already impaired.

text: You are asked to take a random breath test. What happens if you refuse?
options: You are given a warning only
Refusing is an offence, generally treated as seriously as a high-range reading
Nothing, testing is voluntary
You may refuse if you have not been drinking
explanation: Refusing a lawful breath or drug test is an offence in its own right, with penalties comparable to a high-range reading.

text: How do illegal drugs such as cannabis and methamphetamine affect driving?
options: Cannabis is harmless for driving
Stimulants make you a safer driver
They impair judgement, reaction time and perception, and roadside drug testing detects them
Only alcohol is tested for at the roadside
explanation: Illegal drugs impair the judgement, coordination and perception driving depends on, and stimulants add risk-taking and a hard crash afterwards. Roadside oral fluid testing detects several of them.

text: You are a learner driver and drank alcohol at a party last night, stopping at 2am. You need to drive at 8am. What should you consider?
options: It is fine as long as you feel normal
Alcohol may still be in your system, and as a learner you must be at 0.00
Six hours is always enough to be at zero
A large breakfast will clear it
explanation: Your body clears roughly one standard drink an hour, so a heavy night can leave you over the limit well into the next morning. On a learner licence the limit is zero, and feeling fine tells you nothing.

text: Which combination is particularly dangerous for drivers?
options: Alcohol and coffee
Alcohol combined with medication or other drugs
Food and alcohol
Fatigue and fresh air
explanation: Alcohol combined with medication or other drugs multiplies the impairment rather than adding to it. The result can be far worse than either alone, at levels that would seem modest on their own.

text: How does fatigue compare with alcohol as a driving impairment?
options: Fatigue affects only vision
Fatigue is much less dangerous
Fatigue only affects long-distance drivers
Going without sleep for about 17 hours impairs you comparably to a BAC of 0.05
explanation: Around 17 hours awake produces impairment comparable to 0.05, and 24 hours awake is worse than 0.10. Unlike alcohol, there is no legal threshold for it — but the crash risk is just as real.

text: You are planning to drink at an event. What is the best plan?
options: Arrange before you go how you will get home without driving
Drive there and decide later how you feel
Drink only beer, not spirits
Have your last drink an hour before leaving
explanation: Decide before you drink, because judgement is the first thing alcohol takes. Arrange a lift, a taxi or a place to stay in advance.

text: What effect does alcohol have on your ability to judge your own driving?
options: It sharpens self-assessment
It makes you overly cautious
It makes you overestimate your ability while your performance drops
It has no effect on self-assessment
explanation: Alcohol degrades performance and inflates confidence at the same time. That is precisely why 'I feel fine to drive' is not evidence of anything.

text: You are driving at night and your eyes feel gritty and hard to focus. There is no rest area for 40 kilometres. What should you do?
options: Push on to the rest area at the same speed
Pull over somewhere safe and legal as soon as you can, and rest before continuing
Turn on the air conditioning and continue
Increase speed to arrive sooner
explanation: Do not bargain with fatigue over a distance. Stop somewhere safe and legal — a well-lit side road or service station — well clear of the traffic lane, and rest.

text: A friend who has been drinking insists they are fine to drive you home. What should you do?
options: Accept the lift, since they know their limits
Refuse the lift and arrange another way home
Accept if the trip is short
Accept but ask them to drive slowly
explanation: Do not get in. A short trip is when most drink-driving crashes happen, and 'I know my limits' is the impairment talking. Arrange another way home for both of you.

text: Which factor affects how quickly alcohol raises your blood alcohol concentration?
options: Body size, whether you have eaten, how quickly you drink, and drink strength
Only the number of drinks
How much sleep you had the night before
The temperature of the drink
explanation: Body size, food in the stomach, drinking speed and the strength of each drink all change how fast your BAC rises. This is why counting drinks is unreliable — and why zero is the only figure a learner can be sure of.

text: Where must L plates be displayed on a vehicle being driven by a learner?
options: On the windscreen only
On the rear only
Only when driving on main roads
Clearly visible on both the front and the rear of the vehicle
explanation: L plates must be displayed clearly on the front and the rear whenever a learner is driving, so other road users can see them from either direction and give you more room.

text: Who may supervise a learner driver?
