options: A driver who holds a full (not provisional) licence for that class of vehicle
Anyone who has held any licence for six months
Any licensed driver, including a provisional driver
Any adult over 21
explanation: Your supervisor must hold a full licence for the class of vehicle you are driving. A provisional driver cannot supervise you, no matter how experienced they seem.

text: Where must your supervising driver be seated?
options: In the rear seat behind you
In the front passenger seat, beside you
They may follow in another vehicle
Anywhere in the vehicle
explanation: The supervisor must sit beside you in the front passenger seat, where they can see the road, reach the handbrake, and give directions in time to matter.

text: Does your supervising driver need to be under the legal alcohol limit?
options: Yes — the supervisor must be under the legal limit and not impaired
No, only the driver's BAC matters
Only if they intend to drive later
Only on trips longer than an hour
explanation: The supervisor is legally responsible for the driving and must be fit to take control, so they must be under the limit and unimpaired. A supervisor who has been drinking is committing an offence.

text: May a learner driver use a mobile phone hands-free while driving?
options: Yes, for navigation only
Yes, hands-free is always permitted
Yes, if the supervisor holds the phone
No — learner and P1 drivers must not use a mobile phone at all while driving, including hands-free
explanation: Learner and P1 drivers must not use a mobile phone while driving in any way, including hands-free and loudspeaker. Set navigation before you start, or have your supervisor handle it.

text: What must a learner driver carry while driving?
options: Nothing in particular
Their learner licence
A copy of the road rules handbook
Proof of vehicle insurance
explanation: Carry your learner licence whenever you drive and produce it if asked by police.

text: May a learner driver drive alone if the trip is short and local?
options: Yes, if the vehicle displays L plates
Yes, for trips under two kilometres
No — a learner must always be supervised by an appropriately licensed driver
Yes, during daylight hours
explanation: A learner must never drive unsupervised, regardless of distance, time of day or how familiar the route is. Driving unsupervised is a serious offence and voids your insurance.

text: What is the purpose of the learner log book?
options: To record supervised driving hours, which must be completed before progressing
To record any traffic infringements
To record vehicle servicing
To record fuel costs
explanation: The log book records your supervised driving hours, which must be completed and certified before you can progress. Record a spread of conditions — night, rain, highway, town — not just easy trips.

text: What must you pass to obtain your first learner licence in Tasmania?
options: A hazard perception test
A vehicle maintenance assessment
The road rules knowledge test
A practical driving test
explanation: The road rules knowledge test comes first — it is what this app is practice for. Practical driving and hazard perception assessments come at later stages.

text: What colour are P1 and P2 plates in Tasmania?
options: P1 green, P2 red
Both are red
Both are green
P1 red, P2 green
explanation: P1 plates are red and P2 plates are green. Like L plates, they must be displayed on the front and rear of the vehicle.

text: How do demerit point rules differ for learner and provisional drivers?
options: Demerit points apply only to fully licensed drivers
Novice drivers face suspension after accumulating fewer demerit points than fully licensed drivers
Novice drivers are exempt from demerit points
Novice drivers may accumulate more points before suspension
explanation: Novice drivers work to a lower demerit point threshold, so far fewer offences will cost you your licence. Check the current threshold with Transport Services — it is set by regulation and changes.

text: Who is responsible for making sure passengers under 16 are properly restrained?
options: The front seat passenger
The passengers themselves
Nobody, it is a matter of choice
The driver
explanation: The driver is responsible for every passenger under 16 being properly restrained in an appropriate seat or restraint. Passengers 16 and over are responsible for themselves, but the driver should still insist.

text: Your L plate falls off during a drive and you notice at your destination. What should you do before driving again?
options: Write an L on paper and tape it inside the rear window
Drive only on quiet streets until you can buy a new one
Replace the plate before driving again — driving without them displayed is an offence
Continue driving, since it was an accident
explanation: L plates must be displayed and clearly visible whenever you drive. Fit a proper replacement before the next trip; a plate inside the glass or obscured does not satisfy the requirement.

text: Why do learner and provisional drivers have a zero alcohol limit when fully licensed drivers may be under 0.05?
options: Because novice drivers are still building the skills to manage risk, and impairment costs them more
Because novice drivers are more affected by alcohol chemically
Because their vehicles are usually older
Because it is easier to enforce
explanation: Driving is not yet automatic for a novice, so more attention is spent on the basics and there is less left over for hazards. Any impairment costs a new driver disproportionately, which is why the limit is zero.

text: Your supervisor asks you to drive on a busy highway for the first time and you do not feel ready. What is the right response?
options: Refuse to drive at all that day
Drive but stay well under the speed limit in the right lane
Say so, and build up to it with your supervisor when you are ready
Drive anyway, since the supervisor decides
explanation: Supervised practice should stretch you without overwhelming you. Say what you are not ready for and build up in stages — that conversation is part of learning, not a failure.

text: What kinds of driving practice are most valuable to log as a learner?
options: A wide range — night, rain, highways, town traffic, and unfamiliar routes
As many kilometres as possible on the same familiar route
Car park practice only
Only daytime driving in quiet streets
explanation: Variety builds judgement. Hours spent on the same easy route inflate the log book without preparing you for the conditions that actually cause crashes for new drivers.

text: You are a learner and a passenger asks you to read a text message aloud to them while driving. What should you do?
options: Decline — as a learner you must not touch or use a mobile phone while driving
Read it only while stopped at traffic lights
Read it, since you are not sending a message
Read it if your supervisor agrees
explanation: The ban covers using the phone at all, and stopping at lights still counts as driving unless you are parked. Hand the phone to your supervisor.

text: What generally determines how long you must stay at each stage of the graduated licensing system?
options: The class of vehicle you drive
Only your age
A minimum period at each stage, plus the required supervised hours and assessments
How many kilometres you have driven
explanation: Each stage has a minimum holding period plus the hours and assessments you must complete. The time requirement exists because experience accrues with exposure, not just with practice volume.

text: Why do provisional licences carry restrictions such as passenger limits and phone bans?
options: Because new drivers have worse eyesight
Because crash risk is highest in the first year of solo driving, and these conditions target the main causes
To encourage the use of public transport
To raise revenue from fines
explanation: The first year of unsupervised driving carries by far the highest crash risk. Distraction and peer passengers are among the biggest contributors, so the restrictions target exactly those.

text: Where should you check for the current rules that apply to your licence stage?
options: Rules from another Australian state
Social media groups for learner drivers
Whatever your supervisor learned when they got their licence
Transport Services in Tasmania, or the current Tasmanian Road Rules Handbook
explanation: Licensing conditions differ between states and change over time. Transport Services and the current handbook are the authority; another state's rules and a supervisor's memory of the 1990s are not.
